failures.title: Mercedes-Benz OM642 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Oil Cooler Seal Leak (V-Valley O-Ring) - All variants
items.whatHappens: The rubber O-ring sealing the oil cooler, located deep in the V of the engine, degrades over time. This allows oil to leak downwards, pooling on the hot exhaust manifold (creating smoke and a potential fire risk) or dripping onto the driveway.
items.repairVsReplace: The O-ring itself costs under £20, but the labour is intensive (10+ hours) due to the need to remove the intake manifold and associated components. If neglected, it rarely causes catastrophic internal engine damage, but a full replacement is only required if severe overheating or fire damage has occurred.

items.title: Swirl Flap Motor Failure - All variants
items.whatHappens: The plastic gears inside the electronic swirl flap actuator motor strip over time. This causes the ECU to throw a check engine light and default the engine to limp mode, severely restricting power. In some cases, the flaps themselves can seize in the inlet manifold due to heavy EGR soot buildup.
items.repairVsReplace: The actuator motor can be replaced independently and relatively cheaply. However, if the flaps are seized or the manifold is heavily carboned, a full inlet manifold replacement or verified delete is required.

items.title: Turbocharger Seal Leaks - High-mileage units
items.whatHappens: The wastegate actuator or internal turbo seals can degrade, leading to oil consumption, blue smoke from the exhaust, and a noticeable loss of boost pressure.
items.repairVsReplace: Actuator replacement or a turbo rebuild is a straightforward and cost-effective repair. If the turbocharger internals have failed and sent metal debris through the intercooler and into the engine, a full engine replacement is necessary.

failures.goodYearsLine: The OM642 is generally considered a robust and durable V6 diesel. Units maintained with strict oil change intervals and timely preventative replacement of the oil cooler O-ring routinely exceed 200,000 miles without major internal issues .

variants.title: OM642 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: ═══════════════════════════════════════ INTRO: The OM642 family shares the same fundamental 3.0L V6 block and common-rail architecture, but displacement tuning, turbocharging, and calibration vary depending on the chassis. Identifying your exact sub-code ensures you order the correct injection pump, turbo, and ancillary components. - Fitted to: E-Class W211 (E 280 CDI, E 320 CDI), M-Class W164 - Key technical difference: The earlier variant of the OM642 family, typically paired with the 7G-Tronic transmission and featuring a slightly lower output tune. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; early builds are particularly prone to the V-valley oil cooler O-ring leak. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with the .960 high-output variants; the ECU mapping, turbo plumbing, and injection pump calibration differ significantly. - Fitted to: E-Class W212 (E 300 CDI, E 350 CDI), CLS-Class C218, GLK-Class X204 - Key technical difference: A higher-output tune featuring revised piezo-electric injectors in later builds, designed to deliver stronger mid-range torque for heavier saloon and SUV chassis. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; swirl flap motor failure is highly prevalent on this specific tune due to higher EGR flow. - Interchange note: Requires matching ECU and turbo setup; the sump, oil pickup, and engine mounts differ between the W212 and X204 applications. - Fitted to: S-Class W221 / W222 (S 400 CDI), GLE-Class W166 - Key technical difference: The highest output variant, featuring a twin-scroll turbocharger, upgraded cooling systems, and reinforced internal components to handle the increased thermal and mechanical loads of flagship vehicles. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; turbocharger seal wear is slightly more prevalent due to the higher boost pressures. - Interchange note: Cannot be swapped with the .940 or .950 without significant ECU, wiring loom, and hardware changes.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement OM642 Engine - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used OM642 engine makes sense only if it comes with verifiable service history and documented replacement of the V-valley oil cooler O-ring and swirl flap motor. Given the labour-intensive nature of accessing these components, buying a used unit with unknown history often leads to an immediate £1,000+ teardown bill.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned OM642 engine is the sweet spot for most buyers. A reputable rebuild will proactively address the common failure points by replacing the oil cooler O-ring, fitting a new swirl flap motor, and refreshing the turbo seals, giving the engine a fresh lease on life.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full OM642 engine rebuild is justified for high-mileage S-Class or GLE hosts where originality and maximum longevity are required. An upgraded rebuild should include line-boring the block, new pistons/rings, and a balanced crankshaft.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing and fitting through our vetted network ensures your OM642 engine is installed by specialists familiar with Mercedes V6 CDI systems, backed by a nationwide warranty.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: Because the OM642 is typically found in W212, W221, W166, and X204 vehicles valued between £4,000 and £18,000, a full replacement can represent a significant portion of the host's worth. If the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate scrap value before committing .

items.question: What is the difference between OM642.940, .950, and .960?
items.answer: The OM642.940 is the earlier, lower-output variant (found in W211 E-Class), the OM642.950 is the mid-output tune (common in W212 E-Class and GLK-Class), and the OM642.960 is the highest-output variant (fitted to S-Class and GLE-Class).
